Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. Release: datasette 1.0a43

I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone, which is now 53% complete.

The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method.

There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory: private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed).

There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation

excerpt: # Release v5.23.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling2 Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs, and it is intended for use in English and other languages and across multiple coding languages. Its language backbone has 48 mixture-of-experts decoder layers, each routing tokens to 8 of 384 experts, for 594B total and 17B active parameters. It keeps the Inkling decoder (learned relative attention, short causal convolutions, mixture-of-experts layers) and adds block attention residuals, gated attention with a learned sink, and dynamic key/value convolutions. Images are encoded by a Perception Encoder-based vision transformer and projected into the language model embeddings, one embedding per 40x40 pixel patch. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) * Add inkling2 (#50682) by @guarin in [#50682](https://github.com/huggingface/transforme

### Features

* **api:** add source and error codes to the RBAC Role read endpoints
* **api:** add Update Bundle, which sets a Claude Tag Bundle's instructions, and return instructions on Bundle


### Bug Fixes

* **credentials:** write the credentials file on Windows with Python 3.12 and earlier
* **tools:** compare directory names exactly when confining file tool and upload paths on Windows
* **tools:** fully resolve file tool paths that pass through a dangling symlink
* **tools:** ignore ripgrep config files in the agent toolset's grep tool
* **tools:** keep an existing skill directory when the download or extraction that would replace it fails
* **tools:** keep the session tool runner's max_idle countdown running when a session thread terminates

  If the runner fails to read the session's event history after a reconnect, a termination that then arrives on the event stream still cancels the countdown, until the next idle or successful read.

* **tools:** leave symlinks that point outside /memories out of listings
* **tools:** look for ripgrep only in absolute `PATH` entries in the agent toolset's grep tool

  The tool no longer runs an `rg` from a relative or empty `PATH` entry

Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

arXiv:2611.17461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

Abstract: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. excerpt:
arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

arXiv:2611.17339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. arXiv:2611.17398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. arXiv:2611.17412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works
